secondaryFeatures.title: The "Access Hollywood Tape," 10 Years Later
secondaryFeatures.author: Parker Molloy
secondaryFeatures.bodyText:
At 3:03 p.m. ET on Saturday, October 8, 2016, Tic Tac denounced Republican nominee for president Donald Trump.

A day earlier, on October 7, the Washington Post had published a story about a 2005 video of Trump on a hot mic with Access Hollywood host Billy Bush.

“I’ve got to use some Tic Tacs, just in case I start kissing her,” Trump told Bush as they ogled a woman from the set of Days of Our Lives, where Trump was making a cameo. You know the video. We all do. “When you’re a star, they let you do it. You can do anything. ... Grab them by the pussy. You can do anything.”

So yeah, it made sense that a mint brand decided to create some public distance from the soon-to-be-president. And it had company. Sen. John McCain (R-AZ) said he and his wife, Cindy, wouldn’t vote for Trump. Former Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice called on Trump to withdraw. NPR had a running list of Republicans calling on Trump to step aside, and by Saturday night, it had 30 names on it. For that weekend, Trump’s political career seemed to be on life support, and Republicans everywhere were confronting a belief that Trump couldn’t win, and were trying to figure out how to limit the down-ballot damage.

And while that weekend usually gets remembered as the moment we found out that Trump’s claim from earlier in the year that he could “stand in the middle of Fifth Avenue and shoot somebody, and I wouldn’t lose any voters” was more or less true, I’m not positive that’s exactly what happened. The public initially reacted to the tape with genuine disgust. An NBC News/Wall Street Journal poll taken that weekend had Hillary Clinton up by 11 points. And once the tape came out, a number of women came forward to accuse Trump of doing the things he’d been caught on tape bragging about.

This could have been the end of the Trump era. And for one weekend, it looked not just possible, but likely. Ultimately, Trump was bailed out by the Republican Party, which had learned to fear Trump’s biggest supporters, who were uninterested in any talk of Trump dropping out. By Monday, the Republican National Committee was back to being in “full coordination” with the Trump campaign. And by Wednesday, several Republicans who’d withdrawn their support were back on board.

Share

But for one weekend, Republicans told him to quit

The Post’s story went up around 4 p.m. ET on Friday. Trump’s initial response was to dismiss it as “locker room banter,” and then to argue that “Bill Clinton has said far worse to me on the golf course — not even close,” before apologizing “if anyone was offended.” (A real classic of the genre.)

But it seemed to be too late for Trump. Sen. Marco Rubio (R-FL) condemned Trump on Twitter, writing, “Donald’s comments were vulgar, egregious & impossible to justify. No one should ever talk about any woman in those terms, even in private.” Rep. Jason Chaffetz (R-UT) went on Fox 13 in Salt Lake City, saying, “I’m out. I can no longer in good conscience endorse this person for president.”

“My wife and I, we have a 15-year-old daughter, and if I can’t look her in the eye and tell her these things, I can’t endorse this person,” said Chaffetz, adding, “And why should we tolerate this? This is the Presidency of the United States of America: I just can’t do it.”

Trump tried to stop the bleeding by posting a video just after midnight on Saturday.

“I’ve never said I’m a perfect person, nor pretended to be someone that I’m not. I’ve said and done things I regret, and the words released today on this more than a decade-old video are one of them. Anyone who knows me knows these words don’t reflect who I am. I said it, I was wrong and I apologize. I’ve traveled the country talking about change for America but my travels have also changed me. I’ve spent time with grieving mothers who have lost their children, laid-off workers whose jobs have gone to other countries and people from all walks of life who just want a better future. I have gotten to know the great people of our country and I have been humbled by the faith they have placed in me. I pledge to be a better man tomorrow and will never, ever let you down. Let’s be honest. We’re living in the real world. This is nothing more than a distraction from the important issues we’re facing today. We’re losing our jobs. We’re less safe than we were eight years ago and Washington is totally broken. Hillary Clinton and her kind have run our country into the ground. I’ve said some foolish things but there’s a big difference between the words and actions of other people. Bill Clinton has actually abused women and Hillary has bullied, attacked, shamed and intimidated his victims. We will discuss this more in the coming days. See you at the debate on Sunday.”

(That debate, you may remember, was the one where Trump lurked around the stage and threatened to imprison her.)

Nothing was working, and big names in the Republican Party were beginning to rally behind Pence. Trump lost Sen. Mike Crapo (R-ID)’s endorsement on Saturday, with Crapo urging Trump to “step aside and allow the Republican Party to put forward a conservative candidate like Mike Pence who can defeat Hillary Clinton.” Sen. John Thune (R-SD), the future Senate majority leader, pushed for speed: “Donald Trump should withdraw and Mike Pence should be our nominee effective immediately.” Sen. Deb Fischer (R-NE) tweeted, “It would be wise for [Trump] to step aside and allow Mike Pence to serve as our party’s nominee.”

And it looked like the party itself was withdrawing its support, too. That Saturday, Politico reported that the RNC emailed a vendor for its “Victory” program, dedicated to electing Trump, with the subject line “Hold on all projects.” House Speaker Paul Ryan (R-WI) said he was “sickened” by Trump’s comments, and disinvited the future president from an event in Wisconsin that they were supposed to do together.

“With less than a month to go, a major party is walking away from its nominee,” read the headline of an October 8 story in the Washington Post. Brutal! So what happened?

While things didn’t necessarily look great for Trump polling-wise, his “MAGA” supporters were still firmly in his corner, and that made efforts to oust him difficult. On one hand, if you stand by Trump, you run the risk of being seen as a Trump apologist for those comments, potentially losing some voters. On the other hand, if you don’t stand by Trump, you risk alienating his supporters, who you need to win down-ballot races. Ryan got brutally heckled at the Wisconsin event he had disinvited Trump from. “Shame on you!” and “We want Trump!” calls broke out.

A Morning Consult/Politico poll taken right after the story broke found that only 12% of Republicans surveyed thought Trump should end his campaign.1 Seventy-four percent of Republicans wanted the party to continue supporting him. And it looked like the party wasn’t going to have much of a choice, as Trump was adamant that there was “zero chance I’ll quit.“

Most of Trump’s supporters had already baked the creep factor into their support for him. And on the night the tape came out, Ralph Reed of the Faith & Freedom Coalition explained why Trump’s comments wouldn’t be a deal-breaker for evangelicals:

“But people of faith are voting on issues like who will protect unborn life, defend religious freedom, grow the economy, appoint conservative judges and oppose the Iran nuclear deal. ... I think a 10-year-old tape of a private conversation with a TV talk show host ranks pretty low on their hierarchy of their concerns.”

The GOP denounced, then immediately fell back in line behind Trump

On Monday, Ryan told House Republicans that while he wouldn’t personally defend or campaign for Trump, they should “do what’s best for you in your district.” By that evening, RNC chair Reince Priebus told members, “I want to make it very clear that the RNC is in full coordination with the Trump campaign and we have a great relationship with them.”

Things went from “Hold on all projects” to “A great relationship” in 48 hours.

On Tuesday, Fischer walked back her criticism of Trump, telling a Nebraska radio station, “I never said I was not voting for our Republican ticket.” And while that’s technically true, it was just three days earlier that she’d called on him to step aside. Still, sticking with him was “not a tough choice,” she said.

Rep. Scott Garrett (R-NJ) had also called on Trump to drop out of the race over the weekend, but on Wednesday, his campaign said that he “has always said he will vote for the Republican Party nominee.” That week, Thune, Mr. “Effective Immediately,” told a local paper, “I’m certainly not going to vote for Hillary Clinton.”

As Alex Shephard wrote at the time for The New Republic, “Republicans are crawling back to Trump.”

The story didn’t go away, but GOP resistance to Trump did. Had they held firm in defiance of what the MAGA movement was pushing, Republicans would have almost certainly lost the election (the ballots had already been printed and Trump wasn’t going to drop out), but would have been able to tank Trump and regroup for the 2018 midterms and 2020 presidential election with a party built around something other than Trump and his cult of personality. Instead, I think this became the moment when the Republican Party fully surrendered to the Trump wing. Over the following weeks, with a handful of notable exceptions, the party would largely be in Trump’s corner, promoting him as the best available option.

Evangelical theologian Wayne Grudem, who’d withdrawn his Trump endorsement after the tape, was back on Team Trump by October 20, saying, “It isn’t even close. I overwhelmingly support Trump’s policies and believe that Clinton’s policies will seriously damage the nation, perhaps forever.” On October 24, Crapo did a 180, explaining that “the choice we have is between Donald Trump and Hillary Clinton. Given that choice, I will vote for the Republican ticket, Trump and Pence. We must elect a president who will appoint strong Supreme Court justices who will interpret the Constitution as it was written and who will help lead us to a stronger free market economy and a more limited constitutional government.”

On November 1, Ryan told Fox News that he voted early and for the Trump-Pence ticket.

And on the night of October 26, 19 days after declaring “I’m out,” Chaffetz tweeted this:

Two days later, at 12:57 p.m., Chaffetz tweeted again:

That’s how news of FBI Director James Comey’s infamous letter (that potentially won Trump the election) about newly discovered Hillary Clinton’s emails got made public... but that’s a story for another day.

There was never going to be a clean way to get rid of Trump

He was never going to be replaced on the ballot. At least not officially. The day after the Access Hollywood tape came out, CNN reported that replacing him was “practically impossible now because votes have already been cast.”

The party had a decision to make about what it wanted to be. It could sabotage Trump’s election in an act of self-preservation, throwing the election to Clinton, or it could get really comfortable with Trump being the face of the party. It chose the latter, and Trump eked out a win that came down to fewer than 78,000 votes in three states.

The Republicans who briefly condemned Trump have done remarkably well, working their way back into Trump’s good graces. Rubio, who said Trump’s comments were “impossible to justify,” is now the secretary of state. Crapo chairs the Senate Finance Committee. Thune is now the Senate majority leader.

A little more than four years later, Trump would once again find his political fate in the hands of the Republican Party after he tried and failed to carry out an autogolpe. Twice, the party had the opportunity to end Trump’s reign. Twice, it failed to do so, condemning and then welcoming him back with open arms.

1

To put this in perspective, after his disastrous 2024 debate performance, nearly two-thirds of Democrats wanted Biden to drop out of the race.

secondaryFeatures.title: s21e32: Video games are broken; Spotify is less broken; More people have been to Russia...; We actually have an alien?
secondaryFeatures.author: Unknown
secondaryFeatures.bodyText:
0.0 Context setting

Thursday 29 September in Portland, Oregon, where it is dreary but also not raining. Dreary kind of implies rain? Some sort of pregnantly dreary, I suppose. Gravid with rain but not raining yet. Anticipatory.

It’s been just over a week since the last episode and I’ve got to say that every day that I haven’t written I’ve gotten more anxious about not having written. This is not generally speaking helpful because I don’t know about you, but it’s easier to write I’m not anxious. Easier to do anything, really.

I can’t remember if I mentioned, but I got invited to speak at Throughline 2027, Active Voice’s online conference. Here’s some stuff about it:

Join me February 3-5 for two days of talks, one day of workshops, and a whole season of special events centered on this year’s theme: ambiguity as opportunity. I’ll be talking about how to stay intentionally human—and humane—in the time of robots. Early-bird tickets are now on sale through November 8. Get all the details at throughlineconf.com/2027.

I mean it says I’m going to be talking about how to stay intentionally human--and humane--but I’m in the middle of tweaking the talk and also trying not to be anxious about that either. The organizers gave me this feedback about my submission:

Is there a weirder, spicier or more personal place you would go? Someplace thinkier, or that takes a long view and explores some of how we got here as a field? That maybe even ruffles some feathers in a productive way?

... which a) thanks, intimidating, b) thanks, flattered, and c) now having thoughts, thanks.

So that’s another Google Doc that’s staring me in the face.

0.1 How People Work, Live!

Last week I had Michele Tepper on and we exchanged some Strong Opinions, which are always fun, and then for me the interesting bit was where we landed on at the end where I think I feel a bit optimistic about how non-developers/product/designers/engineers are vibe-coding things in organizations?

Michele’s episode and all the other ones are up on the podcast and YouTube now; you can catch up on anywhere RSS works with your podcast app, Apple Podcasts, Spotify, and YouTube.

Next up!

Friday 2 October at 9am PT: How People Work, Live! ... with Hillary Hartley

Hillary Hartley has spent nearly three decades helping government be simpler, faster, and better for the people who rely on it. She started out working with 30 state governments at NIC Inc., then went inside as a Presidential Innovation Fellow and co-founder of 18F, the first digital services team in the U.S. government. She later became Ontario's first Chief Digital and Data Officer, where she built the Ontario Digital Service and wrote the Simpler, Faster, Better Services Act. She was also CEO of U.S. Digital Response, a nonpartisan nonprofit helping state and local governments strengthen their tech capacity. She founded OpenPublic to coach public sector leaders and make transformation stick, and she co-chairs the FWD50 conference. She lives in Toronto with her family, their dog, and a veritable zoo of stuffed animals.

And then after that we’ve got:

  • Friday 9 October: HPW, Live! ... with Jim Ray, currently a founding member of developer relations at Bluesky
  • Friday 16 October: HPW, Live! ... with Farrah Bostic, who runs The Difference Engine
  • Friday 23 October: HPW, Live! ... with Lara Hogan, author and coach, and former VP Engineering at Kickstarter and former Director of Engineering at Etsy

Meanwhile, there’s the open How People Work... Does Happy Hour open clinic on Tuesdays at 1pm PT, where you get to bring what you’ve been thinking about and we chat about it as a small group. I’ve run three of these so far and they’ve all been fun.

1.0 Some things that caught my attention

1.1 Video games are broken

In Edge magazine, The game industry is broken – can we fix it?1, there’s an in-depth story covering the current state of the videogame industry. Some bits that caught my attention:

In 2005, Koster studied the previous decade or so of game budgets, and came to a startling conclusion: “The cost of game development goes up about 10x every decade.” In 2017, he repeated the experiment, this time tapping industry contacts to gather numbers on 250 releases spanning over three decades. This larger data set showed him the very same thing. The cost of making a triple-A console or PC game (accounting for inflation) grew from around $1 million in the mid-’90s to $10 million by 2005, and $100 million by 2015. In the blog post accompanying this research, Koster wrote: “We’re talking one-terabyte games that cost $250 million to develop by the early 2020s”. Today, Sweeney talks about “budgets beginning to hit the $250–400 million level” – figures that line up with those in internal documents that leaked from Insomniac in 2023.1

Essentially, games keep getting more expensive to make, but they don’t actually result in more revenue:

“Since around the year 2000, game budgets have literally doubled every few years,” Sweeney says. “The first Gears Of War, in 2006, cost us $12 million to make, and because we sold six million copies on Xbox, we made $100 million. It was immensely profitable. But, by the end of that generation, as we were making [2011’s] Gears Of War 3, it cost about $100 million to make – and our revenue projection was still about $120 million, because the audience wasn’t growing.”1

All that’s true apart from the live service games, where you get a game that regularly and frequently receives content updates and makes money via subscriptions and also in-game purchases. Epic’s Fortnite is an example of this, but in the article it’s clear that Epic isn’t have a good time of it either.

And all of this is against the backdrop of Microsoft seemingly having no coherent strategy for videogames other than (facetiously) “have a videogame console and lose money over time by spending a lot of money”, see The Xbox reset gets ugly2, from The Verge. (Netflix is also trying to figure out what the deal is with videogames because they’re hitting a limit on attention minutes through video, so need to figure out other valuable things to spend your time on for your subscription)

1.2 Spotify is less broken

Hey, that thing I keep complaining about3, where parents or other people looking after kids would have their end-of-year wrap-ups in streaming music services polluted by obsessive kid music (remember The Year of Moana and The Year of Frozen etc etc) because you couldn’t exclude certain genres or artists? They fixed it! Spotify now has a feature that lets you exclude kids and family music from your taste profile4.

Hmm. People have been asking for this for years. I wonder why it suddenly came out? I mean, Spotify have had a whole bunch of other super important strategic things they’ve been working on, like making sure they own the relationship with your ears. And then video podcasts. And all of that jazz. How come they’ve suddenly got time for this? My hunch is that features like the exclude-genres-to-make-parents-more-sane have always been on the backlog (they’re not stupid, after all), they just haven’t been prioritized. So you don’t get to them unless you’ve got capacity and you really start burning through that backlog of stuff to implement.

Anyway it is by pure coincidence that I happened to read about Spotify’s infrastructure for scaling AI coding agents5 last month. You would be unsurprised to learn that Spotify think they’re doing super great at scaling out agentic coding infrastructure:

The organizations that learn fastest, that compound their engineering knowledge into shared, structured systems rather than leaving it scattered across individuals, will be the ones that capture the full value of AI-assisted development. We have proven that pattern at scale. Now we're shipping that expertise to you.5

If you are the kind of person who is trying to avoid using AI-generated/assisted code, I’m afraid we’re in a post-low-background steel environment6, where ever since we started testing nuclear weapons in the atmosphere the background radiation has been, uh “above normal”. (Don’t worry! It is only slightly above normal now, compared to more than slightly above normal!). There’s a bunch of applications where you want steel to, like, not be that radioactive, so it’s been kind of difficult getting hold of it. People started using the low-background steel analogy a few years ago when ChatGPT came out because it came clear that the internet was going to be poisoned forever by LLM-generated material. Surprise! It has been!

1.3 More people have been to Russia than I have

Yeah, that sentence doesn’t make any sense. Sorry if it broke your brain. I discovered comparative illusion/escher sentences a while back and now you get to see them too.

Caught my attention because: you’re kidding, right?

1.4 We actually have an alien?

I am a big fan of the author Max Barry, especially Company, Jennifer Government, and Lexicon, but most recently via Metafilter7 I cam across Barry’s short story It Came from Cruden Farm published by Slate’s future tense8 which you should read because, well. I cannot give it away. But it was fun. And not fun. I won’t say any more.

That’s it for today! I’m clearly finding it a bit harder to write after a very productive spell. But this episode isn’t really what I thought it was going to be about, either. I suppose this is just how the words come out.

How have you been?

Best,

Dan
